Ingredients

  • 4 cup(s) spinach, baby
  • 1 medium apple(s), Granny Smith, cored and sliced
  • 1/4 cup(s) onion(s), red, thin wedges
  • 2 tablespoon cherries, dried, snipped
  • 1/2 cup(s) cheese, feta, crumbled, (optional)
  • 1/4 cup(s) oil, olive
  • 1/4 cup(s) vinegar, balsamic
  • 2 teaspoon thyme, fresh
  • 1 teaspoon mustard, dijon-style
  • 1/4 teaspoon salt

Directions

Make-Ahead Directions:

Prepare the vinaigrette as directed. Cover and chill for up to 1 week. Serve the leftover vinaigrette with a tossed vegetable salad.

Apple-Spinach Salad:

In a large bowl, toss together spinach, apple, onion, and cherries. Shake Thyme-Dijon Vinaigrette; drizzle onto salad. Toss to coat. If desired, top each serving with cheese. Makes 4 (1-cup) servings.

Thyme-Dijon Vinaigrette:

In a screw-top jar, combine 1/4 cup olive oil, 1/4 cup white or regular balsamic vinegar, 2 teaspoons snipped fresh thyme or 1/2 teaspoon crushed dried thyme, 1 teaspoon Dijon-style mustard, and 1/4 teaspoon salt.

Cover and shake well to mix.

Chill until ready to serve.

Makes 2/3 cup.

No, it does not require coding. Distros is just a term for different Linux versions: Ubuntu, Mint, etc.

They are like a Windows OS. Someone built it for you. Someone did all the coding. It's really, really simple dude.

You download and install. If you have a large hard drive, I recommend partitioning your drive (very easy with windows) and trying it in a quarantined section of your hard drive. That way, you keep Windows which you're comfortable with, and you can fiddle around with the alternative and see if it's for you, rather than giving up before even getting out of bed.

What's the actual benefit of Linux over Windows, specifically?

  • Less viruses
  • Less NSA Probes (potentially, but then again security conscious people might be on Linux so they may target it harder)
  • More customization
  • Lighter, faster OS (most versions of Linux are, anyway)
  • Open source, so even if the one you use, say Mint, gets really bad and starts being all big brother, someone else can step in and make their own version of Mint. Or their own version of Ubuntu. Or they can just branch off and make a radically different Linux-based OS.
  • Free.
  • I don't know how many more reasons you need. Literally the only big thing you lose is PC gaming, and that has been changing for two or more years now.

Don't worry, I'm negative too. I just want you to know that you aren't forced into using something that is trying to abuse you.
